transcript: If Mamma Mia! coming back to Broadway in 2025 isn't a recession indicator, then I don't know what is. Now, because it's essentially the touring production making a stop in New York, I didn't have my hopes high from a production value standpoint, but it was honestly fine. Yes, the set is basically two walls and some furniture that comes in and out, but the cast really fills the stage on their own. In this specific cast, I was really impressed by Amy Weaver who plays Sophie and Jalynn Steele who plays Tanya. Aside from the great vocals, I thought both these actresses brought a spontaneity to their performances that helped keep the show from feeling overly programmed. But even with how formulaic the show is by nature, it's a crowd pleaser for a reason. It moves and maintains a high energy almost the entire time, and you never feel like you're waiting a while for the next song. Overall, this succeeded my expectations — admittedly, I worried it was gonna feel stale and I forgot how fun it is. I do think the ticket prices are crazy, but evidently, people are paying it. And as much as my heart bleeds for the new and original works on Broadway that are struggling to sell tickets, you can't deny that nostalgia sells. I think for a lot of people, there's a nostalgia associated with this musical and with ABBA music in general. I myself fall into that category, but that's a story for another day. With that, another playbill for my collection.
